notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Numbers 15:1–20, drawn from the sources I was able to access.

---

## Numbers 15:1–20 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### Setting and Context

The chapter opens immediately after the catastrophic rebellion of Numbers 13–14, where Israel refused to enter Canaan and God sentenced that generation to die in the wilderness. These laws are given during the wilderness years at Kadesh (Ellicott), and they function as both a supplement to earlier Levitical legislation and a reassurance that God had not abandoned His people or His promise of the land.

---

### v. 1 — "Then the LORD said to Moses"

- **Gill** notes that the Lord spoke "after the murmurings of the Israelites by reason of the spies… and lest their posterity should be discouraged, and despair of ever enjoying the good land." God speaks afresh to assure continuity of the covenant. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-15.html]
- **Pulpit Commentary** observes that the exact date within the wilderness years cannot be fixed. The primary object of these laws was to "supply certain defects and omissions in the Levitical legislation," not simply to encourage the people—though incidentally they did that. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-15.html]
- **Ellicott** notes that "additional laws were given during the long period of the wanderings in the wilderness," which "furnished a practical proof of the continuance of the covenant which had been made with Israel at Sinai." These words were addressed to those under twenty years old at the Exodus—the generation that would inherit. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-15.html]
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: Israel was at one of its lowest points. Yet immediately after the rebellion and chastisement, God gave "valuable examples of God's mercy, care, and help." The style of Numbers 15 mirrors the early chapters, "making a new start with them from the beginning." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-15/]

---

### v. 2 — "Speak to the Israelites… After you enter the land that I am giving you as a home"

- **Gill**: Moses is specifically to speak to the younger generation (those under twenty), since those over twenty were condemned to die in the wilderness. The grant of Canaan is "renewed to them, and an assurance given of their coming into it." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-15.html]
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: The command uses *when*, not *if*—"God had not and would not give up on Israel." These laws contained a built-in promise. "Many a believer under the rod of God's correction has felt abandoned… but God is always near to the believer under correction." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-15/]
- **Pulpit Commentary**: The formula "when ye be come into the land" tacitly assumes two things: (1) burnt offerings and sacrifices would not be offered in the wilderness, and (2) the nation would surely enter Canaan at last. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-15.html]
- **Grant's Commentary**: "His counsels of grace stand because they are founded not on Israel's obedience, but upon that of which the offerings speak, the perfection of the person of Christ and the perfection of His work of sacrifice." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/numbers-15.html]

---

### v. 3 — "an offering made by fire… burnt offering or a sacrifice, for a special vow or freewill offering or appointed feast"

- **Gill** explains that "an offering by fire" is a general term. The burnt offering was wholly consumed on the altar; the "sacrifice" (peace offering) was partly eaten by priests (Deut. 18:1). The three occasions—vow, freewill offering, and appointed feast—all refer to peace offerings (Lev. 7:11ff). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-15.html]
- **Pulpit Commentary**: The burnt offering or slain offering "might be offered in either of these three ways, in addition to the more ordinary sacrifices." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-15.html]
- **Cambridge Bible** notes the expression "a sweet savour" (or "soothing odour") had its origin "in far-off days when the deity was supposed to be soothed or placated by the actual smell of the sacrificial smoke." A trace of the primitive conception remains in Gen. 8:21. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/numbers/15.htm]
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: After their tragic unbelief, Israel "still needed to think about showing gratitude to God for His goodness to them." The grain, oil, and wine expressed thanksgiving. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-15/]

---

### v. 4 — "a grain offering of a tenth of an ephah of fine flour mixed with a quarter hin of olive oil"

- **Gill**: A tenth of an ephah (an omer) was "about three quarts" of fine wheaten flour, mixed with a quarter hin of oil—"a quart and more than half a pint." He adds that this should properly be called a "bread offering" rather than "meat offering." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-15.html]
- **Ellicott**: The meal and drink offering here match those appointed for the morning and evening lamb in Exodus 29:38–40. Meal and drink offerings had already been prescribed for the three great feasts (Lev. 23:13, 18, 37). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-15.html]
- **Pulpit Commentary**: The command to add the grain offering in *every* such case had not been given before, though it was apparently already the practice (Lev. 23:18), following the law of the daily sacrifice (Ex. 29:40–41). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-15.html]
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: Fine flour was "the food of luxury," used in "dainty cooking" (Ezek. 16:13) and "fit for royalty" (1 Kings 4:22). One-tenth of an ephah ≈ two quarts / two litres; one-quarter hin ≈ one quart / one litre. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-15/]

---

### v. 5 — "a quarter hin of wine as a drink offering"

- **Gill**: The wine had to be "wine of the grapes" (per Targum of Jonathan). As sacrifices were "the food of God and the provision of his house, it was proper there should be of every kind fit for an entertainment, as flesh, bread, and wine." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-15.html]
- **Whedon's Commentary (Methodist)**: The drink offering was not drunk by the priest but partly poured out (cf. 2 Tim. 4:6, "I am already poured out as a drink offering"). However, according to Deut. 14:23–27, part of the wine was drunk by the offerer and his family at the peace offering meal. "Hence the inference that bread and wine were, even under Mosaism, the joyous emblems of conscious salvation through the atonement. Wine is a symbol of joy." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-15.html]

---

### vv. 6–7 — The ram: two-tenths ephah flour, third hin oil, third hin wine

- **Gill**: For a ram, six quarts of fine flour with about three pints and a quarter pint of oil. The same quantity of wine as oil. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-15.html]
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: The larger measure for the ram (compared to the lamb) establishes a principle: "the greater our offering, the more joy and gratitude we should bring with it." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-15/]
- **Cambridge Bible** provides a table: Lamb = 1/10 ephah flour, ¼ hin oil, ¼ hin wine; Ram = 2/10 ephah, ⅓ hin, ⅓ hin; Bullock = 3/10 ephah, ½ hin, ½ hin. The amount varies according to the size of the animal. (Measurements: ephah ≈ 1 bushel; hin ≈ 1½ gallons.) [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/numbers/15.htm]

---

### vv. 8–10 — The young bull: three-tenths ephah flour, half hin oil, half hin wine

- **Pulpit Commentary**: The rapid interchange of second and third persons ("he shall bring" / "thou shalt bring") is "awkward and perplexing… No doubt it is due to some sufficiently simple cause in the inditing of the original record… the broken construction remains as a witness to the faithfulness with which the record has been handed down." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-15.html]
- **Ellicott** notes that "in performing a vow" is better rendered "in making a special vow" (cf. Num. 6:2, the Nazirite vow). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-15.html]
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)** ties the "sweet aroma" language to Christ: "The Bible specifically tells us that Jesus Christ fulfilled this sacrifice… Christ also has loved us and given Himself for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling aroma (Eph. 5:2)." The ultimate sacrifice was "perfectly sweet and pleasing to God, and therefore offered once-for-all (Heb. 7:27; 9:12; 10:10)." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-15/]
- **Gill**: According to Jarchi, the drink offering of wine was not a fire offering since the wine "was not put upon the fire." The "offering made by fire" refers to the grain offering and oil only. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-15.html]

---

### vv. 11–12 — "This is to be done for each bull, ram, lamb, or goat… no matter how many"

- **Gill**: The proportion of grain and drink offerings must match the number of animals as well as their individual value. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-15.html]
- **Pulpit Commentary**: The strict proportion "was to be carried out with respect to the numbers, as well as the individual value, of the sacrifices." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-15.html]
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: "Everyone who made a sacrifice had to bring it with the thanksgiving of grain and the joy of wine. God did not want reluctant, complaining people to bring sacrifices to Him. If one could not serve the LORD with gladness (Psalm 100:2), then God didn't want his service at all." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-15/]

---

### vv. 13–16 — The same law for native-born and foreigner

- **v. 13 — "Everyone who is native-born shall prepare these things in this way"**: Ellicott notes the Targum of Jonathan renders this "all that are born in Israel, and not among the people," but from v. 14 it is clear this refers to indigenous Israelites. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-15.html]

- **v. 14 — "if a foreigner residing with you… wants to prepare an offering… he is to do exactly as you do"**: Gill specifies this refers to a "proselyte of righteousness" (a full convert), not merely a "proselyte of the gate." An uncircumcised Gentile might bring burnt offerings, but not with grain and drink offerings. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-15.html]

- **v. 15 — "The assembly is to have the same statute… You and the foreigner shall be the same before the LORD"**: Ellicott renders it literally: "As for the congregation, there shall be one ordinance for you and for the stranger that sojourneth." Some take the opening word as vocative: "O congregation, one ordinance shall be for you and for the stranger." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-15.html]

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**, citing Clarke: "We shall see the absolute necessity of having but one form of worship in the land… no others could be tolerated, because they were idolatrous. All strangers… were required to conform to it; and it was right that those who did conform to it should have equal rights and privileges with the Hebrews themselves." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-15/]

- **Gaebelein's Annotated Bible**: "The stranger is placed upon the same level with the Jew." This "may have a distant view to the calling of the Gentiles in Gospel times." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/numbers-15.html]

- **Gill** likewise sees a Gospel foreshadowing: "This is said to invite and encourage the latter [proselytes], and may have a distant view to the calling of the Gentiles in Gospel times, when there should be no difference between Jews and Gentiles called by grace in matters of religion, but would be one in Christ, Galatians 3:28." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-15.html]

- **v. 16 — "The same law and the same ordinance will apply both to you and to the foreigner"**: Gill adds that this means "one and the same precept to be observed, and one and the same judgment or punishment inflicted in case of non-observance." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-15.html]

---

### vv. 17–18 — "When you enter the land to which I am bringing you"

- **Gill**: This second formula ("whither I bring you") is more emphatic than v. 2 ("which I give unto you"). God assures them that "as he had given it unto them, he would certainly introduce them into it." The Jews later derived from this that the dough-offering law was binding only in the land of Israel and only when all Israel dwelt there. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-15.html]
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: "Even if a child of God isn't walking in the richness of God's promises now, they need to set their mind on heavenly places. Ephesians 2:6 says God has raised us up together, and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-15/]
- **Pulpit Commentary**: This was "a thing which the younger Israelites, few of whom had ever tasted bread, must have eagerly looked forward to (see on Joshua 5:11, 12)." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-15.html]

---

### v. 19 — "you shall lift up an offering to the LORD"

- **Gill**: This was to happen *before* they ate—when they had ground their corn, mixed it with water, and kneaded it into dough. The Targum of Jonathan adds that this applied only to bread from the five grains (wheat, barley, rye, etc.), "not of rice, or millet, or pulse." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-15.html]
- **Pulpit Commentary**: The dedication of first-fruits had been ordered in general terms in Exodus 22:29 and 23:19. Here the specific application to dough from the home is given. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-15.html]
- **Whedon's Commentary**: "Heave offering—Heb. t'roomah, a gift taken from a whole, which one brings to God." It can consist of meat, sin, trespass, or thank offerings, firstborn, tithes, gold, silver, or firstfruits. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-15.html]

---

### v. 20 — "From the first of your dough, you are to lift up a cake as a contribution"

- **Gill**: The quantity is not stated in the Law, so it was "left to the people's generosity." However, according to scribal tradition, it was the 24th part of the first kneaded dough. (He corrects Buxtorf, who mistakenly said the 44th part.) This cake was anciently given to the priest; after the fall of the temple, pious Jews cast it into the fire and burned it. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-15.html]
- **Pulpit Commentary**: The rare Hebrew word *arisoth* (עַרִסֹת) probably means "whole meal coarsely ground, the first preparation of the new corn available for baking and eating." The LXX renders it ἀπαρχὴ φυράματος—the very phrase Paul uses in Romans 11:16 ("If the dough offered as firstfruits is holy, so is the whole lump"). The offering from the home was "in addition to the offering of ears or grains from the threshing-floor." All heave offerings were the perquisite of the priest. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-15.html]
- **Ellicott**: The word *arisoth* is used only here, Nehemiah 10:37, and Ezekiel 44:30, and only in the plural. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-15.html]
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**, citing Cole: "Even the most seemingly mundane daily practice of kneading dough for making bread was to be a time of worship and celebration of God's benevolence and faithfulness." Citing Wenham: "After the fall of the second temple this custom was still maintained: pious Jews would throw a handful of the dough into the fire as a sort of mini-sacrifice, thereby making every hearth an altar and every kitchen a house of God." Citing Allen: "The raising of the first cake of coarse grain is similar to the custom today in small businesses to frame the first dollar. The difference is potent as well; the cake was raised in gratitude to the LORD." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-15/]
- **Gill** notes Paul's allusion to this in Romans 11:16. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-15.html]

---

## Points of Interest Across Traditions

### Differing Emphases Among Protestant Traditions

On this passage, the major Protestant traditions do not differ sharply on the *meaning* of the text, since it concerns ceremonial law. Differences appear in *how each tradition applies it*:

- **Reformed / Covenantal (seen in Gill, Gaebelein)**: Strong emphasis on the covenant continuity—God giving laws after rebellion proves the covenant is intact. The inclusion of the foreigner foreshadows the ingathering of Gentiles (Gal. 3:28). The offerings typify Christ's once-for-all sacrifice.

- **Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / Guzik)**: Emphasises the emotional and devotional dimensions—gratitude, joy, gladness in worship, the "sweet aroma" of a life pleasing to God. The "when, not if" language is applied to believers' confidence in God's promises even under correction.

- **Methodist / Holiness (Whedon)**: Notes the symbolic meaning of bread and wine as "joyous emblems of conscious salvation through the atonement" even under Mosaism—an emphasis on personal experience of salvation and joy that resonates with Wesleyan themes.

- **Brethren (Grant)**: Strong Christological typology: the offerings speak of "the perfection of the person of Christ and the perfection of His work of sacrifice." God's counsels of grace stand on Christ, not Israel's obedience.

- **Baptist (Gill)**: Detailed attention to the precise Hebrew, rabbinic interpretation, and the distinction between proselytes of the gate and proselytes of righteousness. Careful to note the limits of the law's application.

### What Was Not Found

- **Catholic and Orthodox commentaries** (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org): No accessible results were returned within the search constraints for these specific verses.
- **Lutheran sources** (lcms.org, 1517.org): No accessible results.
- **Modern scholarship** (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org): The netbible.org note was briefly cited by Precept Austin ("This chapter collects a number of religious rules") but full notes could not be accessed.
- **Word of Faith / Prosperity / Hyper-grace teachings**: No results were found for this passage from these movements' sources.
